title-group.article-title: Immunogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine prototype based on virus-like particles of hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G and interleukin 12 expressing Semliki Forest virus as a genetic adjuvant

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Virus-like particles (VLPs) based on hepatitis B core antigen (HBc) represent an immunogenic and modular platform for epitope presentation. In this study, the VLPs formed by the modified recombinant hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G (HBc/G) were used as carriers for the presentation of a receptor-binding motif (RBM) of the Delta variant of Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The RBM was inserted at the C-terminus of the modified HBc/G extended by the addition of a second, specifically modified C-terminal domain of HBc/G. All arginine residues in the extra domain were replaced with glycine, resulting in a ‘two-tailed’ HBc/G-Gly vector. The resulting HBc/G-Gly-RBM construct successfully formed regular VLPs in Escherichia coli and elicited specific antibody responses in mice. Despite the moderate immunogenicity of the RBM insert compared with the HBc carrier, sera from RBM-VLP-immunized animals exhibited neutralizing activity against MLV particles pseudotyped with the SARS-CoV-2 Delta spike and showed cross-reactivity with receptor-binding domains from the Wuhan and Omicron variants. To enhance the immune response, a replication-deficient Semliki Forest virus (SFV) vector expressing IL-12 was evaluated alone and in combination with the squalene-based adjuvant AddaVax. The co-administration of SFV-IL12 and AddaVax modestly improved virus neutralization rates and promoted a Th1 response, characterized by increased IgG2a production and IFN-γ secretion. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining classical and genetic adjuvants with the HBc-based VLP platform and provide preliminary insights for further optimization toward more potent and protective SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates.

sec.p: The data presented in this study are contained within the article.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The global challenge posed by emerging viral infections continues to drive the development of adaptable and efficient vaccine platforms. Among these, virus-like particles (VLPs) have attracted significant attention due to their excellent safety profile, structural stability and high immunogenicity [1]. Nevertheless, achieving consistent self-assembly and optimal surface exposure of inserted epitopes on VLPs remains a significant challenge, often affecting the immunogenicity and reproducibility of the final vaccine construct. VLPs based on the hepatitis B core antigen (HBc VLPs) represent a particularly promising platform, having demonstrated utility in the presentation of diverse epitopes in preclinical and clinical settings and have been explored in the context of vaccines against numerous pathogens, including human papillomavirus, influenza and malaria, owing to their robust self-assembly and the capacity to stimulate potent B- and T-cell responses (can be seen in the Table 38.2 of [2]).

The HBc protein consists of two functional domains: N-terminal self-assembly domain (SA, M1–L140), which is sufficient for formation of capsid-like particles (CLPs), as revealed by X-ray studies [2], and a C-terminal domain (CTD) (R150–C183), characterized by arginine-rich sequences responsible for nucleic acid binding and encapsidation [34]. These domains are separated by a hinge region (S141–V149) [5] (Fig. 1a). Since the CTD is dispensable for self-assembly [6], frequently shortened HBc proteins, known as HBc-delta proteins (more often HBc 1–144 or 1–145), have been used in vaccine designs for foreign epitope insertions in the major immunodominant region (MIR), which is the most surface-exposed region of HBc CLPs (for review, see [7]). Some early HBc studies indicated possible alternate localization of the R-rich CTD both inside [8] and outside of the HBc nucleocapsid [910], with cryo-electron microscopy data supporting the interior localization of the CTD [1112]. In contrast to MIR- and N-terminal insertions, C-terminal insertions of foreign sequences generally demonstrate remarkably lower immunogenicity in experimental animals [1314]. However, the extremely high insertion capacity of the C-terminus (up to 559 aa and even 741 aa from HCV [15]) has stimulated further investigations of the C-terminus for modifications of HBc VLPs (for more details, see [7]), and although the CTD is dispensable for self-assembly, its conformation influences the overall properties of the VLP. Structural studies have indicated that CTD localization is predominantly internal; however, modifications of the CTD can alter surface presentation capabilities.

sec.p: The finding that substitution of arginine motifs at the HBc C-terminus with non-charged residues may induce conformational changes in the CTD, thus allowing C-terminal insertions to become more exposed on the HBc VLP surface and thereby more immunogenic, was first demonstrated for the woodchuck hepatitis virus core by David R. Milich’s team [1618]. A special class of HBc VLP carriers, known as HBcG vectors, was constructed by our group to display foreign C-terminal insertions on the surface of structurally unmodified HBc/D capsids [19]. In these vectors, the arginine residues in the CTD were fully or partially replaced by glycine residues. The C-terminal insertion of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) preS1 sequence into this type of HBc-modified carrier protein resulted in the formation of HBc VLPs with exposed 80-aa-long HBV preS1 sequence on the VLP surface and enhanced anti-preS1 response. In that study, a ‘two-tail’ HBc vector was also designed, where the ‘normal’ HBc/D protein was C-terminally supplemented with an additional modified CTD domain, where all arginine residues had been replaced by glycine residues, thus generating the HBc/D-Gly vector (Fig. 1b). In the current study, we employed the same approach to create the ‘two-tail’ vector based on the HBc from the genotype G of HBV, the HBc/G-Gly vector (Fig. 1b). HBc from genotype G was chosen due to the superior expression of this protein in comparative studies with HBc proteins from several HBV genotypes [20]. This novel ‘two-tailed’ hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G (HBc/G) VLP vector was utilized in the current study for the presentation of the receptor binding motif (RBM) of Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Delta variant, in the format of HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs.

The RBM of SARS-CoV-2 viral spike protein was selected for display over the full receptor-binding domain (RBD) for two reasons: first, RBM, particularly involved in host receptor recognition, represents a critical target for neutralizing antibodies and is a frequent focus of vaccine design [2123]. The RBM is responsible for direct interaction with a host receptor, such as angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), and contains the majority of neutralizing epitopes [2426]. Second, as this region typically lacks glycosylation [27], bacterial expression systems can be effectively employed for its production when incorporated into suitable VLP carriers. Nonetheless, RBM sequences alone are often weakly immunogenic, necessitating strategic presentation within immunologically active scaffolds to elicit protective responses. Furthermore, to augment the immunogenicity of such constructs, adjuvants are essential.

A squalene-based adjuvant, such as AddaVax™, an analogue of clinically approved MF59, has been widely used in licensed vaccines and shown to enhance antigen uptake and immune activation [2829]. However, classical adjuvants exhibit several disadvantages, including limited capacity to induce strong cellular immunity, potential reactogenicity and reduced efficacy in elderly or immunocompromised individuals [30]. These limitations highlight the need for innovative immunostimulatory strategies.

Genetic adjuvants, particularly those based on cytokine expression, have emerged as promising alternatives, demonstrating advantages such as sustained local production, targeted immune modulation and reduced systemic toxicity [31]. Vector-based delivery of cytokines, such as IL-12, enables precise orchestration of immune responses by promoting Th1 polarization, enhancing cytotoxic T lymphocyte activity and supporting the development of long-lasting, high-quality antibody responses characterized by the promotion of IgG2a class switching – a factor associated with effective antiviral immunity [3234]. The cytokine-expressing viral vectors offer a potent means of enhancing immune responses not only by the cytokine delivery, but also by the intrinsic induction of innate anti-vector immunity at sites of the vaccine injection. These effects are particularly valuable in the context of antiviral immunity, where both humoral and cellular responses are critical for pathogen clearance.

Replication-deficient Semliki Forest virus (SFV) vectors were shown previously to modulate anti-cancer immune response in murine models by delivery of IL-12, IFN-γ and other cytokines [3537]. The advantages of the replication-deficient SFV vectors include high-transient gene expression, the absence of the vector pre-immunity in a large part of the human population, safety (low pathogenicity) and ability to induce immunogenic cell apoptosis in infected cells [37]. However, the use of SFV vectors as adjuvants for subunits or VLP-based vaccines has been less investigated. The present study explores the immunogenic potential of a novel VLP-based vaccine candidate constructed from the HBc/G ‘two-tail’ vector displaying the RBM motif from a viral spike protein. The immunological enhancement provided by the SFV-IL12 genetic adjuvant, alone or in combination with AddaVax™, was assessed to determine the most effective strategy for eliciting balanced and protective immune responses. Findings from this investigation potentially contribute to the ongoing refinement of modular VLP-based vaccine platforms and support the rational use of combinatory adjuvant approaches in future vaccine development.

sec.title: Bacterial strains
sec.p: Escherichia coli strain BL21 [F−ompT hsdSB (rB− mB−) gal dcm lon] was used for the expression of chimeric HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein and production of corresponding VLPs.

sec.title: Construction of pHBc/G-Gly-RBM plasmid
sec.p: A sequence encoding the 66-aa-long fragment representing the RBM (aa 438–506) of the spike protein of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant (B.1.617.2) was selected for insertion into the Bsp1407I site of a full-length codon-optimized HBc/G-Gly vector. The pET-28a(+) expression vector containing the HBc/G-Gly-RBM fusion protein gene under control of the bacteriophage T7 promoter – the plasmid pET-HBc/G-Gly-RBM – was a commercial product from BioCat GmbH. For the construction of the pBR327-based vector with the HBc/G-Gly-RBM gene under control of the tryptophan operon promoter, the appropriate NcoI/BamHI (Thermo Fisher Scientific Baltics UAB)-treated pHBc183/NcoI expression vector (previously designed for the expression of the HBc/D protein) was utilized [38].

sec.title: Expression of HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein and purification of VLPs
sec.p: Cultivation medium: 300 ml of M9-based mineral medium (g/L: NH4Cl −1.0, KH2PO4 −3.0, Na2PO4 −6.0, pH 7.2) supplemented with 1% Difco™ Casamino Acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 0.2% glucose, 2.5 µg ml−1 thiamine, 2 mM MgSO4 and 20 µg ml−1 kanamycin.

Seed material: overnight culture grown at 37 °C without shaking in standard LB medium (g l−1: Bacto tryptone, 10.0; yeast extract, 5.0; NaCl, 10.0, pH 7.2) with added kanamycin (20 µg ml−1); inoculation rate: 1:100.
Cultivation conditions: cells were cultivated in round-bottomed flasks (0.75 l) on a rotatory shaker at 37 °C for 18–20 h, r.p.m. 200. Final OD540 ~3.2, wet biomass ~1 g from 300 ml.

Collection of biomass: the cell culture was sedimented at 10,000 g at 4 °C for 30 min, and 1 g of cells was resuspended in 20 ml of PBS and transferred to 50-ml Falcon tubes, sedimented again at 10,000 g at 4 °C for 30 min. One gram of cells was then resuspended in 5 ml of disintegration buffer: PBS with DNase I (100 µg ml−1), MgSO4 (10 mM), RNaseA (10 µg ml−1) and Triton X-100 (0.5%) (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with the incubation on ice for the whole disintegration time.

Disintegration of cells: cells were disintegrated with ultrasound using Soniprep 150 (MSE). Resuspended cells were subjected to 5 cycles of 30 s each, amplitude 10 microns, with 5-s intervals for mixing, followed by centrifugation at 14,000 g at 4 °C for 30 min.

Purification of the target protein: (i) gel filtration of supernatant on the XK26/70 column packed with 300 ml of Sepharose 4 Fast Flow (Cytiva) in PBS with 0.05% Triton X-100 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), using the Akta Prime Plus; flow rate 2 ml min−1; (ii) ion exchange chromatography (IEX) of VLP-containing fractions on the XK16/20 column (Cytiva) packed with 20 ml of Fractogel DEAE (M) (Merck) in PBS with 0.05% Triton X-100 as the buffer A and PBS with 1M NaCl and 0.05% Triton X-100 as the buffer B using the AKTA Pure 25 L with two UV 280 nm detectors (Cytiva); flow rate 3 ml min−1. Buffer exchange was performed on the Hiscale16/20 column packed with 25 ml of Sephadex G-25 Superfine (Cytiva) in PBS and 0.5% Triton X-1000; flow rate 2 ml min−1. Column fractions were analysed by SDS-PAGE and native agarose gel electrophoresis (NAGE). The presence of intact VLPs in the fractions was confirmed by immunodiffusion in PBS with 0.8% agarose (Sigma-Aldrich), using in-house polyclonal rabbit anti-HBc antibodies and incubating at 4 °C for 3 days. VLP-containing fractions were combined, and the preparation was characterized by PAGE and NAGE, dynamic light scattering (DLS) and electron microscopy (EM). Protein concentration was measured by the Bradford assay using BSA as a standard.

sec.title: Detection of proteins and nucleic acids
sec.p: The presence of nucleic acids in the protein samples and VLPs was evaluated by NAGE using 1% UltraPure agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in TBE buffer (90 mM Tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane, 90 mM boric acid, 2 mM EDTA, pH 8.3). The NAGE gel was first stained with ethidium bromide (EtBr, UltraPure™, 5 µl of a 10 mg ml−1 stock in 100 ml of PBS) and subsequently with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 (Pierce™, 60 µg ml−1 in 10% acetic acid). Dyes were from Thermo Fisher Scientific.

The protein concentration was determined by the Bradford assay method. The purity of the HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein preparations was evaluated via 15% SDS-PAGE in a Tris–glycine–SDS system, followed by staining the gels with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 according to the standard procedures (LKB Laboratory Manual).

sec.title: Electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering analysis
sec.p: For EM, VLPs in PBS were adsorbed to carbon-formvar-coated copper grids and negatively stained with the 1% uranyl acetate aqueous solution. The grids were examined using a JEM-1230 electron microscope (JEOL) at an accelerating voltage of 100 kV. A minimum of five electron micrographs at a magnification of 100,000 were taken per sample.
DLS was performed using the Zetasizer Nano ZS instrument (Malvern Instruments Ltd. version 6.32), and the ImageJ program was used for the size profiles of the particles in the final product.

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: Baby Hamster Kidney (BHK-21) cells (from ATCCR CCL-1™) were cultivated using Glasgow Minimum Essential Medium (Gibco, Life Technologies) supplemented with 5% FBS (Capricorn Scientific), 10% tryptose-phosphate broth (Gibco, Life Technologies), 2 mM l-glutamine (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific), 20 mM HEPES (Gibco, Life Technologies), 100 mg ml−1 streptomycin and 100 U ml−1 penicillin (Gibco, Life Technologies). Cells were cultured in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂ at 37 °C.

HEK 293 T/17 cells (ATCC, CRL-11268) were cultured in DMEM-GlutaMAX high-glucose medium supplemented with heat-inactivated foetal bovine serum (10%) and penicillin/streptomycin (50 units ml−1, 50 µg ml−1) in 10-cm tissue dishes (all from Gibco).

VeroE6-ACE2-TMPRSS2 cell line expressing human ACE2 and TMPRSS2 was obtained from the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control Research Reagent Repository (UK) and cultured in DMEM-GlutaMAX high-glucose medium supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated foetal bovine serum, 1 mg ml−1 Geneticin (G418), 200 µg ml−1 Hygromycin B and penicillin/streptomycin (50 units ml−1, 50 µg ml−1).

sec.title: Production of SFV-IL12 and SFV-Luc viruses
sec.p: The SFV-IL12 and SFV-Luc virus particles were produced as previously described [3940]. Briefly, the pSFV-IL12 (a kind gift of Prof. C. Smerdou, University of Navarra), pSFV-Luc and Helper-1 plasmids were linearized with the SpeI restriction enzyme (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and 1 µg each linearized plasmid was used for RNA synthesis with SP6 RNA polymerase (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The SFV-transgene RNA and SFV-Helper RNA were co-electroporated into 107 BHK-21 cells using a Gene Pulser-II (Bio-Rad) at 850 V, 25 µF with two pulses. After electroporation, BHK-21 cells were cultured in T75 tissue culture flasks with 15 ml of culture media in a humidified 5% CO₂ incubator at 33 °C for 48 h. After the incubation period, the virus-containing supernatant was harvested and filtered through a 0.22-µm pore vacuum filter (Sarstedt). The SFV viruses were concentrated and purified by ultracentrifugation through the double sucrose cushions (3 ml 50% and 3 ml 20% sucrose in TNE buffer) at 150,000 g at 4 °C for 90 min using the SW 32 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter). The ~2 ml of virus-containing fraction was aliquoted, frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. The virus titre was determined through immunostaining using anti-SFV antibodies (a kind gift from Prof. A. Merits, Tartu, Estonia) and calculated by the infectious unit method, as previously described [41]. Transgene expression was confirmed by the Invitrogen™ IL-12 Mouse ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a Rapid Detection of Firefly Luciferase Activity assay (Promega), following the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Immunization of mice
sec.p: Immunizations of BALB/c mice with purified HBc/G and HBc/G-Gly-RBM proteins were performed as described earlier [42], using female BALB/cOlaHsd mice, 8 weeks of age, obtained from Lanmer OÜ. The experimental procedures were conducted according to the guidelines of the EU Directive 2010/63/EU and local laws and policies. All procedures were approved by the Latvian Animal Protection Ethical Committee of the Food and Veterinary Service in Riga, Latvia (permission no. 136/2022).

All animals were randomly divided into ten experimental groups (n=6) and three control groups (n=3). Mice were injected subcutaneously three times: on days 0, 14 and 28, using different regimens (Table 1). A total of 25 µg of protein in PBS, along with the AddaVax™ (InvivoGen) at a working concentration of 1:1 (100 µl), was injected 8 h after administration of SFV-IL12 or SFV-Luc (50 µl; 5×106 viral particles per injection). A group of non-immunized mice and groups of mice injected with PBS or AddaVax™ alone served as control groups. Animals were bled on days 28 and 42 for serum collection. After day 42, the animals were sacrificed, and spleens were collected (Fig. 2).

sec.title: ELISA for the detection of antigenicity of HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs
sec.p: Nunc 96-well flat-bottom Immuno Polysorp plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated with HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein using 100 µl of protein solution (10 µg ml−1 in 50 mM sodium carbonate buffer, pH 9.6) per well and incubated at 4 °C overnight. Plates were washed three times with PBS containing 0.05% Tween® 20 (PBST) (Sigma-Aldrich) and blocked with 200 µl well−1 of 1% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS at 37 °C for 1 h. The blocking buffer was removed, and wells were washed with PBST four times. Twofold serial dilutions of appropriate polyclonal rabbit antibodies (pAb), starting with a dilution of 1:500 in PBST with 0.05% BSA, were added using 100 µl per well, and plates were incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. After washing with PBST four times, horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (Sigma-Aldrich) was added, 100 µl per well. After incubation at 37 °C for 1 h, plates were washed with PBST four times, and the o-phenylenediamine dihydrochloride substrate (Sigma-Aldrich) was added for the colour development. Absorbance at 492 nm was measured using an automatic Multiskan Microplate Reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The antigenicity of HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs was determined using Rabbit SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) Spike RBD polyclonal antibody (Sino Biological) and in-house rabbit anti-HBc pAb.

sec.title: ELISA for the specificity of induced antibodies against HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs
sec.p: The specificity of mouse sera against the carrier (HBc/G-Gly) and the RBM insert of the HBc/G-Gly-RBM particles was evaluated using the full-length HBc/G (in-house from the LBMC, Riga, Latvia) and three HEK293-expressed RBD reference proteins of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern: (1) SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) Spike RBD-His Recombinant Protein (Wuhan-Hu-1 variant), (2) SARS-CoV-2 Spike RBD (L452R, T478K) Protein (His Tag), (B.1.617.2/Delta variant) and (3) SARS-CoV-2 B.1.1.529 (Omicron) Spike RBD protein (His Tag); all proteins were from Sino Biological. Plates were coated with the reference proteins using 100 µl of protein solution (1 µg ml−1 in 50 mM sodium carbonate buffer, pH 9.6), and serial threefold dilutions of mouse sera starting from 1:50 per well were used. Plates were incubated at 4 °C overnight. All other steps of the ELISA were performed as described above. HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody (Sigma-Aldrich) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The optical density at 492 nm was measured using an automatic Multiskan Microplate Reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

The IgG1 and IgG2a subsets in the sera of the immunized mice were determined using ELISA with Mouse Monoclonal Antibody Isotyping Reagents (Sigma-Aldrich) and a Rabbit Anti-Goat IgG Antibody, HRP conjugate (Sigma-Aldrich).
The end-point titres of antibodies were defined as the highest serum dilution resulting in an absorbance value three times exceeding the absorbance value of sera from non-immunized mice.

sec.title: ELISpot assay of splenocytes from immunized mice
sec.p: At the endpoint of the experiment, the mice were humanely euthanized, and their spleens were excised and homogenized. Single-cell suspensions were prepared using nylon 70 µm cell strainers (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Erythrocytes from the cultures were removed using eBioscience RBC Lysis Buffer (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Freshly prepared spleen cell cultures were tested using the IFN-γ enzyme-linked immunosorbent spot (ELISpot) assay according to the manufacturer’s instructions (MabTech AB). Splenocytes from individual animals in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) medium containing 5% FBS (Gibco) were plated at a density of 5×105 splenocytes per well and stimulated with recombinant HBc/G protein at a concentration of 10 µg ml−1 for 36 h. The cell culture medium (RPMI) was used as a negative control, and the mitogenic agent Concanavalin A (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific), at a concentration of 5 µg ml−1, served as a positive control. The spots formed by IFN-γ-secreting cells were counted automatically using the Immunospot Analyzer S5 (Cellular Technology Limited).

sec.title: Plasmids and production of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles
sec.p: Both the CMV-Gag-Pol murine leukaemia virus (MLV) packaging plasmid encoding the MLV gag/ pol genes (pTG5349-Transgene) and the pMLV-GFP plasmid encoding the MLV-based transfer vector with the CMV-GFP internal transcriptional unit were used as described previously [4344]. A pcDNA3.3-SARS2-B.1.617.2 plasmid, a gift from David Nemazee (Addgene; http://n2t.net/addgene:172320; RRID: Addgene_172320), expressing full-length SARS-CoV-2 B.1.617.2 spike protein (Delta strain), was used for MLV pseudotyping. For this, HEK 293-T/17 cells (ATCC, CRL-11268) were cultured in DMEM-GlutaMAX high-glucose medium supplemented with heat-inactivated FBS (10%) and penicillin/streptomycin (50 units ml−1, 50 μg ml−1, respectively) in 10-cm tissue dishes (all from Gibco). Cells were transfected at 60% confluence with a mix of pTG5349-Transgene, MLV-GFP and pcDNA3.3-SARS2-B.1.617.2 [45] plasmids (8 µg of each) using the calcium phosphate precipitation method (CalPhos™ Mammalian Transfection Kit). Sixteen hours after transfection, the medium was replaced with fresh growth medium (7.5 ml per dish), and the supernatant containing MLV-SARS-CoV-2 Spike-Delta-GFP pseudoparticles was harvested 72 h after transfection, filtered through the 0.45-µm membrane filter, aliquoted, frozen in liquid nitrogen and transferred to −70 °C for storage. Viral titre was quantified using the median tissue culture infectious dose (TCID50) assay, employing MLV-SARS-CoV-2 Spike-Delta-GFP pseudoparticles. Briefly, serial tenfold dilutions of viral pseudoparticles were prepared in complete culture medium and added to monolayers of VeroAce2-TMPRSS2 cells seeded in 96-well plates. Each dilution was tested in eight replicates. After incubation at 37 °C in a 5% CO₂ incubator for 72 h, GFP-positive wells, indicating successful viral entry and reporter expression, were counted using fluorescence microscopy. Viral titres were calculated using the TCID50 calculator (v2.1, 20-01-2017_MB by Marco Binder, adapted @ TWC, University of Heidelberg), based on the Spearman–Kärber method. The titre of pseudoparticle stock used in further neutralisation experiments was determined as 10⁶ particles per millilitre.

sec.title: Neutralization assay
sec.p: To perform the neutralization assay, VeroE6-ACE2-TMPRSS2 cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1×104 cells per well. On the following day, a neutralization assay using MLV-based SARS-CoV-2 pseudotyped particles was conducted with serum samples from immunized mice. Pooled sera from immunized mice (n=6) were analysed at dilutions of 1:10, 1:30 and 1:100 in DMEM. Sera from mice immunized with HBc/G without Gly-RBM protein (vector control) and non-immunized mice sera served as negative controls in the neutralization test. An anti-SARS-CoV-2 Spike/RBD-specific polyclonal antibody (Sino Biological), at a dilution of 1:200, was used as a neutralization control, providing almost complete inhibition of infection. Cells infected with MLV-SARS-CoV-2 particles pre-incubated with cell media only, without mouse serum, served as a positive control for infection.

A virus neutralization assay was performed using pseudotyped MLV-SARS-CoV-2-Delta-GFP particles, which were diluted to achieve a target cell infection rate in the range of 20–30%. The diluted target sera were co-incubated with pseudotyped MLV-SARS-CoV-2 virus at RT for 20 min, and 60 μl of the serum-virus mixture was added to target cells in a 96-well plate. After incubation of the target cells at 37 °C for 5 h, 140 μl of complete cell culture medium was added per well, and the plate was further incubated at 37 °C for 72 h. Infection efficiency was determined by flow cytometry (CytekR Aurora, 5L, Cytek Biosciences B.V) of GFP-positive cells and analysed using FlowJo™ v. 10 software (FlowJo LLC). The percentage of neutralization was calculated as follows: N(y) = (1−y/k) × 100%, where N(y) is the percentage of neutralization, y is the percentage of GFP-positive cells infected in the presence of serum or antibody, and k is the percentage of GFP-positive cells in the positive control – infection with the pseudoparticle preparation alone. Neutralization titre (NT50) values were determined by nonlinear regression analysis using GraphPad Prism software. Neutralization data are expressed as NT50 values, defined as the serum dilution required to achieve 50% inhibition of SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped MLV infection, as determined by nonlinear regression analysis of neutralization curves.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: Mean values were calculated and compared for statistical significance using one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons in GraphPad Prism v8 (GraphPad Software, Inc.). The p-value was considered statistically significant if p<0.05.

sec.title: Expression and purification of HBc/G fusion proteins
sec.p: The EM of purified HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein confirmed the presence of VLPs (Fig. S1A, available in the online Supplementary Material), and DLS of HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs revealed a uniform and homogenous peak of particles with the hydrodynamic diameter (DH) of ~47 nm (Fig. S1B). For comparison, EM and DLS of VLPs for non-chimeric HBc/G protein are given (Fig. S1C, D) with a DH of ~41.5 nm to confirm that, in the case of HBc/G-Gly-RBM, the increased size of the protein monomer results in an enlarged capsid, and the uniform and homogeneous VLP peak in DLS indicates the successful formation of particles.

sec.title: Antigenicity of chimeric HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs
sec.p: Direct ELISA was employed for assessing the specific antigenicity of the obtained chimeric VLPs using the SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) Spike RBD Antibody, Rabbit PAb (Sino Biological), which effectively recognized both the HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein (Fig. 3a) and the eukaryotic-expressed RBD (Fig. 3b) with titres of 1:56,862 and 1:8,000, respectively. Rabbit polyclonal anti-HBc (in-house, LBMC, Riga, Latvia) recognized both the HBc/G-Gly-RBM (Fig. 3a) and the HBc/G protein (Fig. 3c) with titres of more than 1:128,000.

caption.title: The antigenicity of chimeric HBc/G-Gly-RBM by direct ELISA. The following proteins were coated on the plates (10 µg ml−1): (a) E. coli expressed HBc/G-Gly-RBM, (b) Eukaryotic-expressed RBD (Sino Biological) and (c) E. coli-expressed HBc/G. Rabbit pAb against HBc (blue lines) and rabbit pAb against SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) Spike RBD (Sino Biological, red lines) were used as detection agents, as described in the ‘Methods’ section. A twofold serial serum dilution was used, starting from 1:500. A representative result from two experiments is shown.

sec.title: B-cell response
sec.p: To detect the immunogenicity of the HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs, BALB/c mice were primed s.c. on day 0 and boost-injected on days 14 and 28 (vaccination regimens are shown in Fig. 2 and Table 1). Mice were bled on days 28 and 42 to test the induced antibody response against the RBM motif and HBc carrier of the designed HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs (Fig. 4).

caption.title: B-cell response measured by ELISA. (a) Anti-HBc response on days 28 and 42 after the immunization of BALB/c mice with HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs in the presence or absence of the AddaVaxTM and SFV-IL12 virus. Plates were coated with recombinant HBc/G (LBMC, Riga, Latvia) protein (10 µg ml−1). (b) Anti-RBM response on day 42 after the immunization of BALB/c mice with HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs in combination with AddaVaxTM, SFV-IL12 or SFV/Luc as adjuvants. ELISA plates were coated with the following proteins (1 µg ml−1): SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) Spike RBD-His Recombinant Protein, the Wuhan-Hu-1 variant, SARS-CoV-2 Spike RBD (L452R, T478K) Protein (His Tag), the Delta variant B.1.617.2 and SARS-CoV-2 B.1.1.529 (Omicron) Spike RBD protein (His Tag); all proteins were from Sino Biological. The red line indicates the limit of detection. The data are presented as median values (n=6) with 95% confidence intervals. A one-way ANOVA statistical test was performed, and the P-values are indicated on top of the bars. A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant; non-significant P-values are not noted.

graphic.alt-text: Logarithmic plots of antibody responses to HBc/G-Gly-RBM immunization with adjuvants. Data show enhanced HBc-specific IgG and varying RBD-specific responses across coronavirus variants, highest for Wuhan and lowest for Omicron, with significance markers.

sec.p: The anti-carrier antibodies (anti-HBc/G) in the sera of immunized mice were monitored using direct ELISA against two recombinant HBc proteins produced in E. coli or the yeast S. cerevisiae, to clear out the possible influence of E. coli host proteins on the immunological response, as well as antigen adsorption on ELISA plates. The anti-HBc titres of induced antibodies, with coated HBc from E. coli or S. cerevisiae, demonstrated no significant difference (data not shown). Immunization with the ‘naked’ protein (HBc/G-Gly-RBM) showed a difference in the anti-HBc titre detected after immunization on day 28 compared to day 42 (Fig. 4a). In the presence of SFV-IL12, significantly higher titres were observed; however, the difference between days 28 and 42 was not statistically significant. Additionally, no difference between days 28 and 42 was found when AddaVax alone or the combination of SFV-IL12 with AddaVax was used. It is important to note that the antibody titres using AddaVax or SFV-IL12 were very similar and increased the overall anti-HBc titres (Fig. 4a).

At day 42, sera from mice immunized with the HBc/G-Gly-RBM protein were tested in ELISA using RBD proteins from the Wuhan, Delta and Omicron genotypes of the SARS-CoV-2 virus as the coating of the plates (Fig. 4b). In these tests, significantly higher titres were observed against the RBD protein from the same virus variant used for the vaccine construct, the Delta variant, compared to the titres against the RBD proteins from the Wuhan and Omicron variants. However, the inclusion of SFV-IL12 and SFV-Luc as adjuvants did not produce a statistically significant enhancement in antibody titres or in the variant-specificity of the sera from immunized animals. The titres against the Delta and Omicron RBD proteins were higher in the sera of animals that received only AddaVax as an adjuvant compared to those that received a combination of SFV with AddaVax. Furthermore, a broad variability in anti-RBM antibody titres was observed within the groups that received SFV as an adjuvant. For most groups, the differences were not statistically significant; however, when testing the sera against the Omicron RBD, the titres in the group that received AddaVax with SFV-Luc were significantly lower than in the AddaVax-only group. It is noteworthy that the observed anti-RBD response was lower (Fig. 4b) than the anti-HBc response (Fig. 4a). No RBD-specific antibodies were detected in mice immunized with HBc/G as a control (data not shown).

sec.title: Isotyping of IgG antibodies
sec.p: Predominantly, the IgG1 antibody response against the HBc/G carrier was observed for chimeric VLPs containing the RBM, except in the sera of mice immunized in the presence of SFV-IL12. VLPs without the RBM insert induced a predominantly IgG2a response against HBc/G, with the highest response noted in the groups receiving SFV-IL12 (Fig. 5a). The response against the RBD protein remained mostly of the IgG1 type (Fig. 5b). These results indicate that the presence of SFV-IL12 enhances the switch in the anti-HBc/G response from IgG1 to IgG2a.

caption.title: Serum IgG isotype profiles of individual mice on day 42 by experimental group (see group description in Table 1): (a) HBc/G-specific IgG1 and IgG2a levels; (b) RBD-specific IgG1 and IgG2a levels. The IgG1 and IgG2a subsets were determined using ELISA with Mouse Monoclonal Antibody Isotyping Reagents (Sigma-Aldrich). The data are presented as median values with box-and-whisker plots (the box extends from the 25th to 75th percentiles, and the whiskers extend from the minimum to the maximum values). One-way ANOVA statistical test was performed; the P-values are indicated on top of the bars. A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant; non-significant P-values are not noted.

graphic.alt-text: Box-and-whisker plots comparing HBc/G-specific and RBD-specific IgG1 and IgG2a antibody levels in mice. Group 7 shows elevated HBc/G-specific IgG2a. RBD-specific antibodies show higher levels in combined treatment groups versus base vaccine alone.

sec.title: IFN-γ ELISpot test of splenocytes from immunized mice
sec.p: The level of T-cell activation in the spleens of immunized animals was tested with an IFN-γ ELISpot assay evaluating the number of IFN-γ-secreting cells in response to Ag stimulation. A significant enhancement of the response to specific stimulation with the recombinant HBc/G protein in animals co-immunized with SFV-IL12 and SFV-Luc was observed (Fig. 6). The increased number of IFN-γ-secreting cells in stimulated splenocytes (with RPMI as a control) from animals that received SFV-IL12 and SFV-Luc indicates immune system activation through the expression of the IL-12 cytokine and the response to the SFV backbone vector. ELISpot analysis was performed using only the VLP carrier, as the RBM region does not contain experimentally confirmed T-cell epitopes in BALB/c mice; therefore, RBD-specific stimulation of splenocytes was not performed.

caption.title: IFN-γ ELISpot analysis of splenocytes from immunized mice. Splenocytes from a group of mice (n=6) were isolated and cultured in the presence of HBc/G protein as a stimulating Ag for 36 h. The spot-forming cells (SFC) per 106 splenocytes were counted. (a) Total number of SFC in mock-stimulated and specifically stimulated splenocytes, RPMI control refers to the culture medium (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific). (b) Specific response to a stimulating Ag (HBc/G protein) after subtracting the SFC number corresponding to non-specific stimulation with RPMI control. The data are presented as individual values (n=6) and median. One-way ANOVA statistical test was performed; the p-values are indicated on top of the bars. The value of P<0.05 was considered statistically significant; non-significant P-values are not noted; a double asterisk (**) indicates P<0.01, a triple asterisk (***) indicates P<0.0001.

graphic.alt-text: IFN-γ ELISpot scatter plots comparing immune responses in immunized mice. SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/Addavax induced significantly stronger splenocyte responses with approximately 2,000 spot-forming cells per million splenocytes.

sec.title: The ability of sera from immunized mice to neutralize SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped MLV particles
sec.p: To evaluate the functional capacity of the induced antibodies, a neutralization assay using SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped MLV particles was performed. The virus neutralization assay revealed that the best inhibitory effect was achieved in all groups where RBM containing VLPs was present (Fig. 7). At a serum dilution of 1:10, virus neutralization rates of around 80% were observed and showed statistically significant differences (P<0.005) compared to the control group vaccinated with HBc/G/AddaVax, where the virus neutralization rate was around 50%. Notably, the PBS control groups also demonstrated a non-specific neutralization effect at this low serum dilution, equivalent to ~60%. A similar trend was observed at a 1:30 serum dilution, where all groups receiving HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs showed significant virus neutralization compared to controls, achieving the highest rate of 69.99% in the SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group. Nonetheless, a non-specific neutralization effect was still present in the PBS group, equivalent to 24.57%. A dose-dependent effect was evident in groups receiving HBc/G-Gly-RBM, exhibiting virus neutralization at a 1:100 serum dilution. The non-specific neutralization effect observed in the control group at 1:10 and 1:30 serum dilutions disappeared at a 1:100 dilution, allowing a clearer assessment of the specific neutralization effect. Interestingly, at a 1:100 dilution, only the HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax and SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax groups showed statistically significant inhibition compared to the control HBc/G/AddaVax group. Moreover, the neutralization rate of 38.4% observed with the Ab from the SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group was statistically different from all other groups immunized with HBc/G-Gly-RBM, indicating a synergistic effect of the SFV-IL12 and HBc/G-Gly-RBM in the immunization. At a 1:100 serum dilution, the SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group exhibited significantly higher neutralization capacity compared to the HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group (P=0.0013), highlighting the IL-12’s adjuvant effect. Neutralization titre (NT50) values for groups with AddaVax were calculated by plotting the percentage of pseudovirus inhibition against serum dilutions and fitting the data using a nonlinear regression model (Fig. 7d, e). The highest NT50 was observed for SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group (1:65), compared with SFV-Luc+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax (1:26) and HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax alone (1:39). While the SFV-IL12 supplemented group showed superior performance, all formulations containing the RBM immunogen remarkably outperformed the baseline neutralization levels observed in the control groups HBc/G/AddaVax (1:12) and the AddaVax/PBS control (1:10). The neutralization levels in these control groups likely represent non-specific background activity characteristic of low serum dilutions. Because sera were pooled for neutralization analysis, NT₅₀ values represent group-level approximations and were not subjected to ANOVA statistical comparison based on biological replication. Overall, the neutralization results demonstrate that RBM-containing VLP formulations induce measurable neutralizing activity, with higher neutralization observed in formulations incorporating SFV-IL12, although overall NT₅₀ values remained modest.

caption.title: Neutralization of pseudotyped MLV-GFP/SARS-CoV-2-Delta virus by sera from immunized mice. Neutralization was performed at a serum dilution of (a) 1:10, (b) 1:30, (c) 1:100. (d) Neutralization curves used for NT50 estimation. (e) NT50 values for the indicated groups. Serum from animals within each group was pooled (n=6), preincubated with MLV-GFP/SARS-CoV-2-Delta virus at respective dilutions, and then the virus was used for VeroE6-ACE2-TMPRSS2 cell infection. The cells expressing GFP as a reporter of infection were quantified by flow cytometry, and neutralization was calculated as the proportion of infected cells with respect to the control (infection without any serum). GraphPad Prism was used to present data from three independent experiments (n=3). Data are shown as mean±sd (A–C). One-way ANOVA test was used for group comparison in panels (a–c); the respective P-values are indicated. NT50 values were calculated using a non-linear regression analysis (d) and are presented with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) (e). The red dotted line in panel (d) indicates 50% neutralization.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: VLPs, being highly immunogenic per se, additionally offer significant advantages in recombinant vaccine design as a platform for high-density display of foreign antigens of choice on the VLP surface by genetic or chemical approaches [7]. Such high-density presentation is believed to facilitate B-cell activation and antibody production crucial for protective immunity [4651]. HBVHBc VLPs have often been used for antigen presentation (can be seen in Table 38.2 of [2]). While the MIR of HBc is considered optimal for surface display due to its location at the tips of surface spikes formed by the bundle of eight alpha-helices of HBc [2], our previous work demonstrated that RBM insertions into the MIR, although capable of inducing relatively strong B-cell response, often disrupted VLP integrity due to the physicochemical properties of the insert. The hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity of the inserted sequence and the proximity of the N- and C-ends of the insert affect the structural stability of the VLPs [4252].

The current study employed VLPs formed by the HBc protein from HBV genotype G (HBc/G), selected by us for superior expression of HBc/G VLPs in E. coli compared to HBc variants from other HBV genotypes [20]. For the presentation of the RBM of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant on HBc/G VLPs, a ‘two-tailed’ HBc vector designed by us earlier [19] was employed in this study. This vector incorporates a modified, glycine-rich C-terminal extension of HBc to spatially separate the RBM inserted at the C-terminus of the extended HBc to preserve the conformation of the RBM insert while retaining the VLP-forming ability of the chimeric construct. The resulting HBc/G-Gly-RBM VLPs demonstrated the capacity to induce RBM-specific antibody responses in immunized mice, although these responses were lower than those elicited against the HBc carrier. Importantly, the elicited antibodies displayed measurable functional neutralizing activity against MLV particles pseudotyped with the SARS-CoV-2 Delta spike (Fig. 7) and demonstrated cross-reactivity with RBD proteins from Wuhan and Omicron variants (Fig. 4). While RBM-specific immune responses were clearly detectable, the titres and neutralizing activity remained modest. Arginine-containing ‘one-tailed’ HBc/G-RBM construct with RBM inserted into the MIR was not included in this study because the fusion protein of this kind was unable to form VLPs [42], and, therefore, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the superiority of the ‘two-tailed’ HBc/G-Gly vector (with glycine-modified second tail) vs. ‘normal’ ‘one-tailed’ HBc vector for RBM insertion.

Adjuvants play a vital role in enhancing immune response, particularly when dealing with subunit or VLP-based vaccines containing poorly immunogenic components. Classical adjuvants like AddaVax, a squalene-based oil-in-water emulsion similar to MF59, are known to enhance antigen uptake and presentation [53]. However, such adjuvants may lack the ability to sufficiently stimulate robust cellular immunity, particularly Th1 responses, and can be associated with reactogenicity/toxicity or reduced efficacy in vulnerable populations [5455]. The exploration of novel immunostimulatory strategies, particularly cytokine-based genetic adjuvants, represents a promising direction in vaccine development.

In this context, IL-12 has previously been proposed as an adjuvant for inducing antigen-specific immunity against various pathogens and cancers, typically administered as a recombinant protein [5657]. To our knowledge, the current study represents a first attempt to use the virus vector for the transient expression of IL-12 as an adjuvant for the protein-based vaccine. IL-12 is known to promote Th1-type immune responses, increase IFN-γ production and drive class switching to IgG2a [58]. SFV vectors offer additional immunostimulatory effects through their RNA-mediated activation of innate immune sensors [5961], which augment local inflammation at the site of administration and thereby reinforce vaccine-induced immunity. In this study, ELISpot assays showed that co-administration of SFV-IL12 significantly enhanced anti-HBc IgG2a responses and IFN-γ secretion, indicative of a Th1-related immune profile. The increased number of IFN-γ-secreting cells in stimulated splenocytes (with RPMI medium as a control) from animals that received SFV-IL12 indicates the activation of the immune system through the expression of the IL-12 cytokine and the response to the SFV backbone vector. These findings are consistent with earlier studies demonstrating IL-12’s capacity to enhance the Th1 responses and shift antibody subclass profiles in the context of other antigens [3233 62 63].

It has been shown that IgG2a plays an essential role in protection against pathogens by enhancing opsonization, complement fixation and other immune effector functions. The IgG1-to-IgG2a class switch enables a more effective immune response tailored to the specific type of pathogen encountered; therefore, the induction of IgG2a antibodies may be crucial for the development of effective vaccines and immunotherapies by improving protective immunity [64]. Interestingly, while the HBc-specific response exhibited a strong IgG2a bias under the influence of IL-12, the anti-RBM response remained predominantly of IgG1 type, suggesting less efficient engagement of the Th1 pathway. This may be attributed to intrinsic characteristics of the RBM motif, such as the lack of T-cell epitopes, which may favour a Th2-biassed response. These observations highlight the significance of specific epitopes within the chimeric VLP construct in influencing immune polarization and underscore the need for further optimization.

Combining SFV-IL12 with AddaVax further enhanced the magnitude and quality of the antibody response. At a 1:100 serum dilution (Fig. 4a), the HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group showed neutralization rates of ~20%, while the SFV-IL12+HBc/G-Gly-RBM/AddaVax group achieved rates of 38%, indicating a synergistic effect of both AddaVax and SFV-IL12. In this study, the SFV-IL12 vector was administered 8 h before the injection of VLPs, combined with AddaVax in order to minimize potential interference of AddaVax with SFV-mediated infection; however, further optimization in combining viral vectors with conventional adjuvants will be necessary to consider in future studies. Nevertheless, the data suggest that AddaVax may contribute to improved antigen retention and presentation, while SFV-IL12 boosts cellular responses and antibody isotype switching, resulting in a more balanced and durable immune profile. The observed animal-to-animal variability in the immune response may be attributed to several factors. In particular, a certain degree of structural or conformational instability of the chimeric VLP construct in vivo may affect antigen presentation efficiency and, consequently, the magnitude and quality of the immune response. In addition, even minor genetic differences and variations in the physiological or immune status of the animals can lead to differences in the composition and functional activity of immune cells. Importantly, the variability in anti-RBM responses among mice receiving SFV-IL12 suggests that while the vector is effective in boosting Th1 responses, its impact on certain immunogens may not be predictable. This finding supports the notion that genetic adjuvants like SFV-IL12 vector may be more effective when paired with structurally optimized, inherently immunogenic targets like HBc. Furthermore, other cytokines, such as IL-4 (for Th2 stimulation) and TNFα (for immune cell attraction and inflammation), should be additionally considered as potential adjuvant genes.

For protective immunity, vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 should generate a long and effective T-cellular response, apart from the production of neutralizing antibodies [65]. IFN-γ is often utilized as a cytokine endpoint in ELISpot assays and has a wide range of biological functions in the context of an immune response, including the activation of macrophages, up-regulation of major histocompatibility complex I and II and induction of IgG production from activated B cells [66]. In this context, it is established that IL-12 plays a dominant role in IFN-γ induction. Following priming with SFV-IL12, elevated levels of IFN-γ were detected in ELISpot assays stimulated with HBc protein (Fig. 6), consistent with the observed IgG1/IgG2a ratio in sera from immunized mice. Given these results, the incorporation of CTL epitopes derived from SARS-CoV-2 structural proteins, such as the nucleocapsid (N) protein, into HBc-based VLPs represents a promising strategy for future vaccine development in combination with SFV/IL12 for broader and more durable cellular immunity.

In summary, our study demonstrates the feasibility of employing the HBc/G-based VLP platform for the presentation of the conformational SARS-CoV-2 RBM domain and highlights the beneficial effects of SFV-IL12 as a genetic adjuvant for Th1 stimulation. The observed shift in antibody isotypes, increased IFN-γ production and found viral neutralization underscore the potential of this approach in eliciting a balanced and protective immune response. Nevertheless, although sera from immunized animals displayed measurable neutralization activity against SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus, the NT₅₀ titres remained relatively low. This suggests that the C-terminally presented RBM, while accessible to the immune system, may not be optimally exposed or presented at a sufficient density on the VLP surface to induce high titres of functional neutralizing antibodies. These findings, therefore, emphasize that further structural optimization – such as modifying linker length or insertion site – will be needed to enhance the accessibility and immunogenic potential of the RBM on the HBc/G platform. Overall, future research should focus on exploring alternative adjuvant combinations and conducting in vivo challenge studies using the K18-hACE2 transgenic mouse model, which recapitulates key features of viral replication and lung pathology observed in human Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), to fully establish the durability of the antibody response and protective efficacy of the vaccine [6768]. Despite the modest anti-RBM antibody response and neutralization activity observed in this study, our findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining an HBc-based VLP platform with a virus-encoded genetic adjuvant to enable surface presentation of a conformational SARS-CoV-2 RBM and to modulate the quality of the immune response, providing a foundation for further structural and immunological optimization.
